groups.title: API design: layered architecture and validation
groups.question: Your Express routes contain SQL, validation and business rules all mixed together, and bad data sometimes reaches the database. Explain how you would structure the backend and validate input.

followUps.Service and repository layers for separa: What does each layer do: route, controller, service and repository?
followUps.Input validation at the API boundary pre: Why validate at the API boundary instead of deep in the code?

evidence.text: Routes map URLs, controllers handle the request and response, services hold business rules and repositories run database queries.
Each layer depends only on the one below it.
This lets you change the database code or reuse business rules without rewriting everything.
All incoming data is checked as soon as it enters the API.
A validation error there gives a clear message about which field is wrong.
Business logic and the database only ever see valid data.

groups.title: Caching and query optimization
groups.question: Your recipe API is slow under load: clients re-download the same lists and one endpoint makes a query per recipe. Explain how caching and query optimization help.

followUps.HTTP caching: Cache-Control, ETag, and c: How do Cache-Control and ETags reduce work for clients and the server?
followUps.Database query optimization: indexes, EX: How would you find and fix a slow query?

evidence.text: Cache-Control tells clients and proxies how long they may reuse a response.
An ETag identifies a version of a resource.
Clients send the ETag back, and if nothing changed the server replies 304 without the body.

notEnough: Only saying caching makes things faster.

evidence.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows how the database runs a query, such as scanning the whole table.
Adding indexes on filtered and joined columns speeds them up.
Loading related data in one query instead of one per row removes the N+1 problem.

groups.title: Input validation, rate limiting, and security headers
groups.question: Your login endpoint is being hit by thousands of password guesses, and a security scan flags missing headers and unvalidated fields. Explain how you would harden the API.

followUps.express-validator for chained field vali: How does express-validator check fields, and what should the route return when they fail?
followUps.Helmet for security headers and express-: What do Helmet and a rate limiter protect against?

evidence.text: Validators are chained per field, such as checking an email is valid.
The handler checks the validation result before doing any work.
If there are errors, it returns 400 or 422 with the list of problems.

notEnough: Only saying you validate with a library.

evidence.text: Helmet sets security headers that protect against attacks like clickjacking and some injection.
A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a time window.
Strict limits on login slow down password-guessing attacks.

groups.title: Logging and monitoring basics
groups.question: Your API crashed overnight and the only logs are scattered console.log lines with no context. Explain how you would log and handle process-level errors.

followUps.Structured logging with pino or morgan: Why use structured JSON logs instead of plain text?
followUps.Process error handlers: uncaughtExceptio: What should happen on an uncaught exception or unhandled rejection?

evidence.text: Structured logs write each entry as JSON with named fields.
Log tools can search, filter and graph by fields like request id, user and status.
Libraries like pino are built for fast logging in production.
The process listens for uncaught exceptions and unhandled promise rejections.
It logs the error and shuts down cleanly.
The app should not keep running after an uncaught exception, because its state may be broken, and a process manager restarts it.

notEnough: Only saying you catch all errors.

misconceptions.text: Says the app should log the uncaught exception and keep running.
